commit.message:
[grug] Benchmark the June Snowball trainer on synthetic tokens (#9693)

`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py` runs the June
67B-A2B recipe's own trainer and model on synthetic tokens from one
Slurm node, with no Fray or Iris, so the Grug code path can be measured
on AMD GPUs (#9462) against Levanter's `SnowballConfig`. It builds the
production model through the recipe's width heuristic with the cooldown
launch's switches, feeds fresh uniform-random examples through
`LmDataConfig` with a mixture block the length of the dataset so nothing
repeats and the loss stays a leak check, and takes the same flags as the
Snowball harness: presets, steps, batch, expert axis, mixed-precision
policy, attention and MoE implementation, and a profile window.

The June trainer always created a checkpointer and force-saved the final
state, about 1 TB for the 67B model. `GrugTrainerConfig` gains
`save_checkpoints`; False skips the checkpointer entirely.

Measured on the AMD HPC Fund cluster at the full 67B shape on 8 GPUs,
one 4096-token sequence per GPU, bf16 or fp16 compute with f32 params:
MI350X bf16 FSDP 9.57 s per step (0.29% MFU), MI350X fp16
expert-parallel 1.09 s (2.59%), MI350X bf16 expert-parallel with the
Triton `ragged_dot` 0.73 s (3.86%), MI300X bf16 FSDP 2.27 s (2.19%),
MI300X bf16 expert-parallel about 0.76 s (6.5%). These agree with
Levanter's `SnowballConfig` through the #9613 harness within about 10%.
Details are in the baseline comment on #9462.

commit.message:
Score the first 4k Paloma PTB tokens in hero vibe checks (#9776)

Add `paloma-ptb-first-4k` to the hero vibe-check prompt bank, following
https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8827#issuecomment-5723229156.
It tracks how the hero scores Paloma's Penn Treebank (PTB) text across
sampled checkpoints.

The prompt is the first line of Paloma's `ptb` validation document, a
single 399,782-character document with 87,132 tokens under the Marin
tokenizer. The prompt is 17 tokens including BOS. The `expected`
reference is the next 143 lines, or 4,056 tokens. With EOS, the prompt
and reference total 4,074 tokens, within the sampler's 4,096-token
`context_length`. Existing expected-answer scoring reports per-token
probabilities and the total log-likelihood of the first ~4k PTB tokens
at every sampled checkpoint. No code changes are needed. PTB is
lowercase, with numbers replaced by `N` and rare words by `<unk>`, so
the score partly measures in-context adaptation to that format.

Changing the prompt bank changes the sampling specification and creates
a new request for every retained checkpoint. The hourly workflow in
`next` mode keeps two jobs active, newest first. Steps 210000 and
204000, the two newest permanent checkpoints of
`hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k`, are sampled first. Older checkpoints
backfill afterward at the saved priority.

All 47 prompts passed the sampler's prompt-prefix and context checks
locally with the pinned tokenizer revision.
`tests/hero_vibe_check/test_completions.py` had 19 passing tests.
`./infra/pre-commit.py` passed on the changed file.

commit.message:
[grug] Select the hero router's top-k experts with a Triton kernel

XLA:GPU uses its own top-k kernel only for rows of at least 1,024 elements, so the hero router's
top-(K+1) over 384 experts lowers to a full sort of every row, run in the forward and again in the
recompute. At [65536, 384] that costs 0.856 ms per call in isolation and 1.22 ms per call in a hero
step trace.

A Triton kernel, called through jax_triton, now holds one row in one warp, as one power-of-two tile
or, when that pads less, three equal ones (a 384-wide row is three 128-wide tiles with no padding),
and takes k successive maxima over XLA's float32 total-order key, breaking ties by the lower column.
Its indices and their order match jax.lax.top_k for every input, including ties, signed zeros,
infinities and NaNs of either sign. A taken or absent entry gets the smallest key and the column n,
which the lowest-column reduction never returns, so a negative NaN with payload 0xFFFFFFFF, whose
key is also the smallest, cannot be confused with a taken entry. The kernel reads an int32 view of
the input, so autodiff never asks the call for a JVP rule. For k above 16 the steps run in a loop:
unrolled steps run 6% faster at k = 9 but compile in 36 s at k = 384, against 0.2 s for the loop.
Float32 rows of fewer than 1,024 entries on a GPU device take the kernel; everything else keeps
jax.lax.top_k. The hero's QB router reads its threshold alpha back from the logits at the (K+1)-th
index, the value jax.lax.top_k returned there.

One warp per row keeps both reductions inside the warp. Triton 3.6 reduces across warps through
shared memory twice, with three barriers per reduction, so a row split over two warps runs slower.
An earlier version of this kernel held four rows in four warps per program and tracked taken entries
with per-entry masks, which spilled to general registers: 1,016 SASS instructions per warp at k = 9,
against 736 with no barriers and no shared memory now.

The kernel's gate asks the default device whether it is a GPU (levanter.grug._moe.availability)
instead of calling jax.default_backend(). A hero test stubs jax.default_backend to trace a GPU-only
attention path on CPU devices, and under that stub a backend check would select the kernel there.
The Triton gather-sum's gate moves to the same check. The GPU tests compare the kernel bitwise with
jax.lax.top_k over widths 1 to 1023 in one or three tiles, padded or exact, k up to 37 and NaN
payloads, and run it inside a shard_map that checks varying axes, as the hero calls it.

Per call on one GB200, [65536, 384] float32, timed in one job (median of 5 interleaved runs, each 16
calls on distinct inputs in one jit; CUPTI kernel time, median of 20 calls, in parentheses), in ms.
Earlier Triton is the four-row version above; Pallas is a port of the same algorithm, which compiles
through XLA's Triton pipeline, and is not kept.

| k | jax.lax.top_k | Earlier Triton | Pallas | This kernel |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 9 | 0.856 (0.798) | 0.125 (0.102) | 0.105 (0.084) | 0.096 (0.074) |
| 8 | 0.856 (0.798) | 0.114 (0.091) | 0.096 (0.076) | 0.089 (0.066) |

On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), the earlier Triton kernel
shortened the step from 12.943 to 12.875 s (+0.53%).

commit.message:
[grug] Let rematerialization discount the hero's host-offloaded carry

With the layer carry offloaded to pinned host memory, XLA's post-schedule
HloRematerialization still charged the 36 GiB carry stack against the device
memory limit, so it recomputed ~10 GiB of backward values per step that already
fit in HBM (143 remat clones, 0.63 s/step of compute, including a synchronous
attention-weight all-gather per layer). `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading`
makes it count host buffers as host memory. The flag is read only by the remat
pass, which runs after scheduling and copy insertion, so it cannot reorder the
carry reload against its consumer. It becomes an overridable default whenever
the carry is offloaded.

commit.message:
[grug] Run ragged collectives synchronously without the carry offload

A ragged run without the carry offload keeps XLA's latency-hiding scheduler off, and the collective
overlap limit binds only that scheduler. XLA's default scheduler starts collectives regardless of
the limit. Compiled for a mocked 64-GPU EP64 topology (8 hero layers, the launcher's flags for this
configuration), the program already holds two ragged transports in flight at once: the first
chunk's return beside the second chunk's dispatch in the forward, and a cotangent dispatch beside a
recomputed dispatch in the backward. On GB200, several collectives in flight have hung the ragged
transport or given run-to-run different gradients.

The launcher now forces --xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES for this configuration
and drops any value the caller set. Compiled the same way, the program then runs one collective at a
time. The hero's carry-offload flags are unchanged.

commit.message:
[grug] Build PGLE latency profiles for hero diagnostics

From #9481. With collective overlap limited to one, XLA's latency-hiding scheduler decides how much
communication hides under compute, and its default estimator gives every collective the same small
latency, so it treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under one GEMM. `pgle_profile`
turns one XProf trace of the hero train step into a ProfiledInstructionsProto of measured
instruction costs for `--xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`, and the README describes the
trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE stays off, since it cannot profile with one process per
GPU.

On one rack restored from step-180000, a profile built from the program's own trace (3678
instruction costs) shortened the step of the hero with every change from #9708 from 12.611 to
12.515 s (+0.77%). The profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it
was traced from.

commit.message:
[grug] Stop zero-filling and overwriting the ragged MoE transport buffers

The expert chunks write disjoint rows of the dispatch and return buffers, but
the custom VJP around `ragged_all_to_all` differentiated each write as an
overwrite, so every layer's backward spent a [TK, H] select, a [TK, H] add and
a [TK, H] zero fill on rows the next chunk would ignore. On inputs that are fresh
at the written rows, the overwrite has the derivative of an add, so the transpose
now passes the output cotangent through unchanged.

With every consumer reading only rows a collective wrote, the transport buffers
need no fill at all. They come from a Triton kernel that writes nothing (zero
filled off GPU), tied to a loop-carried value so XLA keeps them inside the layer
loop. Dropped and padded slots get combine weight 0, and the combine and
dispatch-gradient sums skip them.

Outputs, drops and every gradient are bitwise equal to the previous commit
across drops, padding, one-hot routing and hero per-shard shapes on GB200x4;
one MoE layer's forward and backward is 4.4-4.8% faster, and the compiler temp
drops by 1.37 GB per layer.

commit.message:
[grug] Scatter token rows once into the ragged MoE dispatch buffer

On GPU, a Triton kernel now builds the expert-sorted dispatch buffer by reading each token's row
once and writing it to the token's accepted sorted slots. The gather it replaces,
x_local[sorted_indices // topk], reads every source row topk times. The other slots stay unwritten;
the transport reads only accepted slots. Off GPU, one gather still fills every slot. The kernel can
also scale each written row by a per-assignment fp32 weight, rounding once, for the routed-expert
backward's weighted output cotangents.

The gather-sum's forward kernel now loops over 1024-wide hidden tiles instead of one tile as wide as
the backward's, which keeps more programs resident. Each element still sums its K rows in order, so
the result is unchanged.

On GB200 at TK = 524288, H = 3072, the scatter takes 0.535 ms (6.6 TB/s), and the gather-sum
forward takes 0.508 ms against 0.574 ms with one 4096-wide tile.

commit.message:
[grug] Test that the ragged MoE reads no unwritten transport rows

The ragged transport buffers start with unspecified contents, and each consumer is meant to read
only rows a collective wrote. Unit tests poison the rows each consumer skips, but the end-to-end
GPU tests run the real allocator, whose rows are often zero, so a new reader of an unwritten row
could pass them while reading stale values in training.

The new GPU test runs the ragged layer with forced drops and padding, once with every transport
buffer zero-filled and once NaN-filled. Outputs, drop counts and all gradients, including a
recompute, must be finite and bitwise equal between the two. The recompute takes a fresh function
for each fill, because jax.checkpoint caches its trace by function and would otherwise keep the
first fill.

commit.message:
[grug] Compute the MoE routing-weight gradient on the expert side

The routing-weight gradient dS[t,k] = <dout[t], y[t,k]> was the only backward
consumer of the expert down projection's output y. Since dy = w * dout and
dh = dy W2^T, the same value is rowsum(dh * h) / w, built from tensors the
expert MLP backward already holds. One custom VJP from dispatch to combine now
returns s = <h, dh> per expert row (fused into the SwiGLU backward), sends it
back with one [C, 1] f32 all-to-all per chunk, and forms dS = s / w in f32;
dropped and padded slots get 0 by selection, not division.

Where w * dout rounds to zero in the cotangent dtype (a zero weight, or in
float16 a normal weight times a small cotangent), the row's cotangent carries
nothing and dS comes out zero or inexact, so the expert-side gradient is an
opt-in: RoutingWeightGradient.EXPERT_SIDE on moe_mlp and MoEExpertMlp. The
default, EXACT, keeps the returned expert outputs and differentiates the
combine, which is exact for any weight. The hero selects EXPERT_SIDE: its
routing weights are positive renormalized sigmoids and its cotangents bf16,
which has fp32's exponent range.

With y unneeded in the hero, the offload_carry remat policy saves the routed
output before the latent up projection (18 GiB across 48 layers), and the

times its routing weight, rounded once. On GPU it now comes from the dispatch scatter kernel's

scatter, with the gather-sum retiling, shortened the step from 12.875 to 12.730 s (+1.14%). That

+"""Build an XLA:GPU PGLE latency profile from one XProf trace of the hero train step.

+program with measured instruction costs. XLA's default estimator gives every collective the same
+small latency, so it hides a multi-millisecond ragged transport under a single GEMM. The profile

+import tempfile

+    """``tensorflow.profiler.ProfiledInstructionsProto``, which jaxlib does not export."""
+    proto = descriptor_pb2.FileDescriptorProto(name="profiled_instructions.proto", package="tensorflow.profiler")
+    message = proto.message_type.add(name="ProfiledInstructionsProto")
+    string, double, optional, repeated = (
+        descriptor_pb2.FieldDescriptorProto.TYPE_STRING,
+        descriptor_pb2.FieldDescriptorProto.TYPE_DOUBLE,
+        descriptor_pb2.FieldDescriptorProto.LABEL_OPTIONAL,
+        descriptor_pb2.FieldDescriptorProto.LABEL_REPEATED,
+    )
+    cost = message.nested_type.add(name="InstructionCost")
+    cost.field.add(name="name", number=1, type=string, label=optional)
+    cost.field.add(name="cost_us", number=2, type=double, label=optional)
+    latency = message.nested_type.add(name="Latency")
+    latency.field.add(name="source", number=1, type=string, label=optional)
+    latency.field.add(name="target", number=2, type=string, label=optional)
+    latency.field.add(name="latency_us", number=3, type=double, label=optional)
+    message_ref = descriptor_pb2.FieldDescriptorProto.TYPE_MESSAGE
+    message.field.add(
+        name="costs",
+        number=1,
+        type=message_ref,
+        label=repeated,
+        type_name=".tensorflow.profiler.ProfiledInstructionsProto.InstructionCost",
+    )
+    message.field.add(
+        name="latencies",
+        number=2,
+        type=message_ref,
+        label=repeated,
+        type_name=".tensorflow.profiler.ProfiledInstructionsProto.Latency",
+    )
+    pool = descriptor_pool.DescriptorPool()
+    pool.Add(proto)

+

+        # The converter reads a TensorBoard profile directory: <run>/*.xplane.pb.

+        fs, path = filesystem_for(xplane_uri)
+        fs.get(path, os.path.join(run_dir, "trace.xplane.pb"))
+        serialized = profiler.get_profiled_instructions_proto(run_dir)
+    profile = _profile_message_class()()
+    profile.ParseFromString(serialized)
+    if not profile.costs:
